newsitem.title: GREECE: Hard drachma policy intact despite turbulence.
newsitem.headline: Hard drachma policy intact despite turbulence.

text.p: The hard drachma policy, Greece's main anti-inflationary policy tool, successfully passed yet another test this week with the highly visible ecu/drachma rate fluctuating in the 309.50-310.25 band.

"There is no doubt that the central bank is backing full-heartedly the hard drachma policy," said the chief forex dealer at a foreign bank. "Even those who sell drachmas for ecus or other currencies know that."

The Bank of Greece has announced it wants the drachma broadly stable against the main currencies that make up the ecu this year. It delivered on its hard drachma policy pledge in 1996 by letting the drachma slide by only 1.0 percent against the ecu.

The Bank of Greece wants to reduce inflation to 4.5 percent year-on-year by the end of 1997 and push it below 3.0 percent by end-98. Consumer price inflation was running at 5.5 percent year-on-year in June.

Foreign and local players started buying large amounts of ecus, dollars and marks for drachmas late on Tuesday, culminating in outflows of 660 million ecus and $60 million at the fixing on Wednesday. The resulting liquidity squeeze helped drive interest rates up in the money market.

The central bank intervened repeatedly to satisfy the strong demand for foreign currencies at the fixing on that day and at its afternoon window signalled to the market that it would not let the ecu/drachma rate surge to levels incompatible with its end-year inflation goal.

Dealers estimated forex outflows have totalled in excess of $1.0 billion in the last few days. A large local bank bought 100 million marks for drachmas at the fixing on Friday pushing ecu/drachma slightly above 310.

The first challenge to the strong drachma policy came in late May when London-based banks either closed out positions or opened new ones, usually combining drachma borrowing through forex forwards with foreign currency buying at the fixing.

The combination did not have much of a lasting effect on the ecu/drachma rate due to the central bank's intervention. But it did drain funds out of the money market driving interest rates higher, at times above 12 percent.
The higher cost of funding and the turmoil which adversely affected market sentiment hit government bonds, pushing yields higher.
Ecu/drachma pierced the 312 level in late May before the central bank intervened to prop up the national currency and reverse the upward trend in ecu/drachma.
The resulting outflows, estimated at $2.0 billion or more, helped reduce its foreign exchange reserves to $16.3 billion at end-May from over $18 billion at end April.

Some dealers and analysts have pointed to the deterioration in the country's current account deficit, up 35 percent to $1.627 billion in the first quarter of 1997 compared with the same month last year, and the drachma's prospective participation in the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) as causes for concern.

But others have said the current account deficit was still under control, below 4.0 percent of gross domestic product, and the fight against inflation was a priority for both the government and the central bank, permitting no slippage in the hard drachma policy.

"The participation of the drachma in the ERM might be one of the prerequisites for the EMU (European Monetary Union) but so are lower inflation and the budget deficit and the latter ones take priority," said a foreign bank dealer. "ERM can wait, inflation reduction cannot."
A Reuters poll among Greek bankers conducted last spring showed that the vast majority of them expected the drachma to join the ERM in 1999. -- Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
